analysis.one_liner: Restricts debt collection tactics, medical debt credit reporting, and collection of student loans after death or disability.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on December 18, 2024, with no cosponsors, referred to the House Financial Services Committee, and died there without a vote when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal debt collection law in nine sections. It would ban confession-of-judgment clauses in small business lending, bar debt collectors from threatening service members with rank reduction or security clearance loss, require private student lenders to cancel loans when a borrower dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled, stop credit bureaus from reporting medical debt for a year (and never for medically necessary care), limit collectors' ability to barrage consumers with texts, emails, and social media messages, cap fees private collectors can charge when collecting government debts at 10 percent of the amount collected, increase and inflation-index penalties for illegal collection practices, and stop private collectors from pursuing FEMA disaster aid overpayments except in cases of fraud. The bill never moved past its initial referral to committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers dealing with debt collectors, small business owners, active-duty service members and recent veterans, families of deceased or disabled private student loan borrowers and their cosigners, people with medical bills, and disaster survivors who received FEMA overpayments by mistake.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, service members, borrowers, small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Bans lenders from using confession-of-judgment clauses and warrants of attorney against small business borrowers — clauses that let a lender seize a business owner's assets without notice or a day in court [S2].

Prohibits debt collectors from threatening service members with rank reduction, security clearance revocation, or military prosecution — threats that exploit service members' fear of career damage [S2].

Requires private student loan holders to discharge a loan when the borrower dies or is totally and permanently disabled, including releasing cosigners (typically parents) from liability, and bans ongoing collection attempts afterward [S2].

Bars collection activity on a medical debt for two years after the first payment is due, prohibits credit bureaus from reporting any debt for medically necessary care at all, and blocks reporting of other medical debt for at least 365 days — giving people time to resolve insurance disputes and hospital financial assistance before their credit is damaged [S2].

Makes it an unfair practice for collectors to barrage consumers with unlimited texts, emails, and social media messages without direct, specific consent, and requires the consumer agency's debt collection rules to prohibit unlimited electronic contact [S2].

Caps fees charged by private collectors hired by federal and state agencies at 10 percent of the amount collected and requires those agencies to give consumers three written notices, spaced at least 30 days apart, before turning a debt over to a private collector [S2].

Raises the penalties for violating the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act — including tying the cap to 5 percent of a collector's gross annual revenue — indexes them for inflation for the first time, and adds injunctive relief for consumers, making violations costlier for repeat offenders [S2].
Bars Treasury from hiring private collectors to recover mistaken FEMA disaster aid payments unless the overpayment resulted from fraud the recipient knew or should have known about [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Third-party debt collection agencies, consumer credit bureaus, private student loan lenders and servicers, and lenders that rely on confession-of-judgment clauses would bear new legal exposure, lost collection fees, and written-off balances. Some compliance costs could be passed to consumers through higher prices or tighter lending terms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Debt collectors, credit bureaus, private lenders

drawbacks.text: Mandatory discharge of private student loans on death or total permanent disability would be a new loss lenders must absorb, and they would likely price that risk into loans for all future borrowers, raising borrowing costs for students who never qualify for a discharge [S2].

Blocking all collection on medical debt for two years and barring credit reporting for medically necessary care indefinitely would shift more unpaid provider costs onto hospitals and insurers, which could pressure them to demand larger upfront payments or more aggressive charity-care screening [S2].

Restricting collectors' electronic communications while requiring federal rules to prohibit unlimited contact would raise compliance and staffing costs for collection firms, costs that flow through to creditors and potentially to consumers in the form of higher prices on credit products [S2].

A good-faith objection: bundling nine separate titles into one bill meant none of the individual measures received independent committee scrutiny, hearings, or amendment before the Congress ended [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protections target practices with well-documented harm — medical debt ruining credit scores before insurance disputes are resolved, collectors threatening service members' careers, and small business owners losing assets without a hearing. The tradeoffs are real but narrow: private lenders would reprice discharge risk, and providers would face slower medical debt recovery. The bill is a broad one-sided expansion of consumer rights, and its main weakness is procedural — it was dropped in the final two weeks of a session with no cosponsors, so none of its nine parts were debated on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two weeks of the 118th Congress and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it stayed until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Maxine Waters, the ranking Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the bill on December 18, 2024 [S1].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Financial Services the same day; that was the only action ever taken on the bill [S4].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without a vote, and all bills die when a Congress ends [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collection firms, credit reporting agencies, private student loan lenders, and small business lenders using confession-of-judgment clauses all avoided the new restrictions, fee caps, and increased penalties the bill would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors, credit bureaus, private lenders

for.name: Maxine Waters

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee hearing or markup on the bill; it remained at the referral stage for the bill's 16-day life.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without action from December 18, 2024, until the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred and no other member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no partisan positioning on the merits.

industries.note: The bill caps their fees on government contracts at 10 percent of collections, restricts texting and social media tactics, requires more notice before debts are transferred to them, and raises penalties for violations. Firms that profit from aggressive contact volume and fee stacking would lose revenue and face higher legal exposure.

The bill bans reporting of medical debt from medically necessary care outright and blocks other medical debt from appearing on reports for at least a year. Bureaus currently sell reports containing medical collections, a leading driver of credit score damage for tens of millions of people.

industries.industry: Private student loan lenders and servicers
industries.note: The bill requires them to cancel loans when a borrower dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled and to release cosigners, ending a practice of pursuing grieving or disabled families for balances.

industries.industry: Small business and merchant cash advance lenders
industries.note: The bill bans confession-of-judgment clauses — contract terms that let a lender obtain a judgment against a business owner without notice or a court hearing — removing an enforcement shortcut some high-cost lenders rely on.
